Triggers.value: Visible injuries or wounds on others

Maladaptive Strategies.value: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous
Any form of physical contact with others

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

Negative Appraisals.value: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power
I am permanently an outsider now
People are not what they seem

issues.explanation: The trigger pattern is only partly coherent with the trauma type and the rest of the profile. Nausea and visible injuries fit partner physical abuse, but darkness is a more context-specific trigger that is not supported by the memory or appraisal items; no item suggests assaults occurring in dark spaces or fear linked to darkness specifically.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Public Transport: Using public transport
issues.explanation: Avoiding public transport is hard to explain from the rest of the profile. None of the trigger, memory, or appraisal items point to buses/trains/crowds/public transit as trauma-linked cues, so this strategy appears to target a symptom context not otherwise represented in the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Male Presence: Being alone with men
issues.explanation: For trauma type 'physical abuse by romantic partner,' the trigger 'being alone with men' is hard to reconcile unless the abusive partner was male and the fear generalized specifically to men; demographics/trauma description do not support that specificity, so this item is clinically questionable.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'People can't be trusted' is very broad and non-specific, while the trigger pattern is specifically male-coded. That combination is not impossible, but here it weakens coherence because the profile gives no corresponding trauma-linked reason for a male-specific trigger alongside a fully generalized interpersonal belief.

Within the Memory node, 'hard to deliberately recall' and 'memories are very clear and detailed' can coexist in PTSD, but in this profile they are phrased in a way that risks direct contradiction unless the distinction between involuntary vivid intrusions and impaired voluntary recall is explicit. A clinician would likely question whether these two items were selected to describe the same memory pattern without additional clarification.

vignette: The assault happened on a Tuesday in November, when the humidity had given way to a brittle cold. At twenty-six, Elias had come home to find his girlfriend drinking heavily, her breathing shallow and erratic. When he reached for her arm to guide her to the couch, the alcohol smell hit him first, sharp and cloying. She shoved him backward. He struck his head against the drywall, hearing a sickening crack before his vision swam. What followed was a blur of strikes and kicks, the wet thud of his own ribs against the floorboards, the copper taste of blood pooling under his tongue. He lay there until she finally threw a ceramic mug against the wall and stormed into the bedroom, leaving him with a split lip, a purple bruise blooming across his collarbone, and a wave of nausea so violent he retched into the hallway rug. He fled the apartment that night, but the trauma did not stay behind. Within weeks, the precinct coffee machine became a minefield. Every time the barista frothed milk over the distinct, yeasty scent of spent beer, Elias felt his stomach drop, a sudden wave of nausea mirroring the one on his floorboards. That physical lurch did not pass unnoticed; it pulled the assault into sharp focus, his mind replaying the crunch of the mug shattering and his own desperate pleas with perfect, unfiltered clarity. The memories refused to sit quietly. They forced their way into his focus during roll call, vivid and uncontrolled, stripping away any distance between past and present. As the sensory echoes of that night multiplied, so did his conviction that the world had fundamentally shifted. He began to see every interaction through the lens of sudden violence. The smell of stale drinks in break rooms, the sight of a colleague's bruised knuckles from a basketball game, even a raised voice in the hallway-all of it confirmed a new, rigid belief that people are never as they appear and that he is permanently an outsider in his own life. That isolation, in turn, acted as fuel for the intrusions. Because Elias had come to believe that no one could be trusted and that safety was an illusion, his brain stopped filtering out threat. The negative appraisal that he was permanently on the outside made the traumatic memories feel more urgent, more real, and impossible to dismiss. The uncontrolled access to those vivid, sensory-laden recollections then dictated his daily behavior. He stopped trying to process what happened, opting instead to shut down completely. He began to emotionally numb himself, treating his feelings as liabilities rather than signals. When his wife, Sarah, reached out to hold him after a hard shift, he would stiffen and step back, avoiding being touched because any physical contact felt like the prelude to violence. He also refused to relax, lying awake on the couch with the television blaring or pacing the floors, convinced that letting his guard down was dangerously close to being caught off guard again. These defensive habits quickly calcified into a self-reinforcing trap. By consistently avoiding relaxation and cutting himself off emotionally, Elias found himself increasingly isolated from his wife and his partner's support network. This withdrawal cemented his belief that he was an outsider, reinforcing the distrust that had kept him in survival mode. He was certain that the emotional numbing meant to protect him instead left his nervous system chronically hyper-aroused, meaning that minor environmental shifts-like the clink of keys at the door or a heavy footstep on the stairwell-readily triggered that familiar wave of nausea and sensory flashbacks. He had tried to manage the threat by building walls, but those walls only narrowed his perception of danger, making the triggers feel omnipresent and inescapable. At work, his hyper-vigilance bled into his investigations; he started doubting the credibility of informants without cause, pushing away veterans who tried to debrief with him, and ultimately calling in sick three days in a row after a routine domestic dispute call left him frozen in the squad car, unable to speak. What finally brought Elias to my office was the night Sarah left his keys on the counter and walked out, telling him she could not live with a ghost. He realized the numbness and avoidance were not shielding him from the past but erasing his present. He now sits across from me, hands folded tightly in his lap, bracing for the next intrusion while quietly hoping that therapy might teach him how to stop bracing. He fears that if he finally lets go of the hyper-vigilance, the nausea and the memories will overwhelm him completely, but he is desperate to find a way back to a life where he is not waiting for the next blow.
